vignette:
Patient: Fatima, Age 21  
Occupation: Database Administrator  
Trauma Type: Military (Non-Combat, Sexual Assault by a Superior Officer)  
PCL-5: 79  

Fatima is a slight young woman with dark, watchful eyes that seem to scan the room even when she is sitting still. She was referred by her primary care physician after a series of panic attacks at work, but she has been reluctant to talk about what happened. Over several sessions, the story has emerged slowly, in fragments.

She enlisted at eighteen, eager to escape a controlling family situation and to prove she could be independent. Basic training was brutal but she loved it-the structure, the physical challenge, the sense of purpose. She was assigned to a logistics unit as a data systems technician, responsible for maintaining personnel databases. She was good at it. Her supervisors praised her attention to detail.

It happened during a six-month deployment. Her direct supervisor, a Staff Sergeant in his late thirties, began singling her out for "extra training sessions" in the evening. At first, it was just uncomfortable proximity, comments about her appearance. She told herself she was being oversensitive. Then one night, he cornered her in the supply room, locked the door, and raped her. She did not scream. She had been trained to be silent, to follow orders, to not make a scene. Afterward, he told her that if she told anyone, her career would be over, and no one would believe a private over a decorated NCO.

Fatima did not tell anyone. She buried it. She finished her deployment, completed her service, and was honorably discharged eighteen months ago. She now works as a database administrator for a mid-sized tech firm. On paper, she is doing well-she has her own apartment, a steady job, no debt. But inside, everything has collapsed.

She cannot sit with her back to a door. In her cubicle, she has arranged her desk so that she faces the entrance to her aisle, and she has hung a small mirror on her monitor to see who is approaching from behind. The sound of a man clearing his throat-a specific, phlegmy sound-makes her freeze. She once dropped a cup of coffee and had to lock herself in the bathroom for twenty minutes, shaking.

Her sleep is a disaster. She goes to bed at 11 PM but lies awake until three or four, replaying the supply room. The smell of dust and cleaning solvent. The lock clicking. The weight. She has nightmares almost every night, but they are not literal replays. In the dreams, she is drowning in a sea of server racks, cables wrapping around her legs, and a voice over an intercom repeating her social security number. She wakes up gasping, her sheets soaked in sweat.

She has stopped dating entirely. The thought of physical intimacy makes her stomach turn. She deleted her dating apps months ago. When a male coworker touches her shoulder to get her attention, she flinches. She has started working from home three days a week to avoid the office, but even there, she is not safe. The sound of a delivery truck backing up-a beeping sound that reminds her of the base-makes her heart race.

She has become hypervigilant about her data. She triple-checks every entry, terrified of making a mistake that will get her in trouble. She stays late to recheck her work, unable to trust her own memory. Her manager has noticed her declining productivity and has scheduled a "performance conversation" for next week. Fatima is terrified. She is convinced she is going to be fired, that she is incompetent, that everyone can see she is broken.

She has not told anyone about the assault. Not her mother, not her friends, not her therapist-until now. She says the words slowly, as if testing them for poison. "He said no one would believe me." She looks down at her hands. "And he was right. I don't even believe myself sometimes."

She is not sure why she is here. She does not think talking helps. But she cannot keep living like this, either.
